stem: A 3-year-old boy who lives in a house built in 1920 has been irritable, with crampy abdominal pain. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, MCV is 70 fL and ferritin is normal. The smear shows coarse blue dots in many red cells.
oneliner: 3M + 1920 house + irritability + abdominal pain + MCV 70 + normal ferritin + coarse blue dots in red cells → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his anemia?

whyNot.A: Iron deficiency has a **low ferritin**; his is normal
whyNot.B: Thalassemia minor does not cause **abdominal pain and irritability**, and its smear shows target cells
whyNot.C: Lead can itself leave ringed sideroblasts, but the best answer names the cause: **old paint, colic, irritability and coarse stippling** point to lead, and he has no alcohol, isoniazid or inherited cause
whyNot.D: Chronic disease needs a **long inflammatory illness**; he has none

why: Lead **inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase**, so heme is not made and the cells are small. It also blocks the RNA-degrading enzyme, leaving **coarse basophilic stippling**. Old paint, colic and behaviour change complete the picture.

head: Ferritin
Serum iron and TIBC
Smear
Deciding test or setting
rows: Pencil cells, high RDW, low red cell count
Menstrual or GI blood loss, pica
**Low iron with low TIBC** (iron trapped in macrophages)
Long inflammatory illness or cancer; high hepcidin
Target cells, red cell count high for the hemoglobin
Normal or high iron (iron cannot enter heme)
Old paint or firing range; abdominal pain, neuro signs
**Ringed sideroblasts on marrow iron stain**; alcohol, isoniazid, ALAS2

also: Zinc protoporphyrin and ALA rise; treat with succimer or EDTA

stem: A 45-year-old man taking isoniazid for latent tuberculosis has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL and MCV is 72 fL. His conjunctivae are pale and the platelet count is normal. Sideroblastic anemia and iron deficiency anemia are both being considered.
oneliner: 45M + isoniazid + Hb 9.8 + MCV 72 + pallor → sideroblastic or iron deficiency?
ask: Which single finding favours sideroblastic anemia over iron deficiency anemia?

whyNot.A: **Small cells** occur in both; it is why they are confused
whyNot.C: The **degree of anemia** does not separate them
whyNot.E: **White cells** are normal in both; neither condition touches them

why: Isoniazid uses up **vitamin B6**, the cofactor of ALA synthase, so heme cannot be made and iron is not used: **serum iron and transferrin saturation run high**, and the marrow shows ringed sideroblasts. In iron deficiency transferrin saturation is very low (often below 10%).

head: Ferritin
Serum iron and TIBC
Smear
Deciding test or setting
rows: Pencil cells, high RDW, low red cell count
Menstrual or GI blood loss, pica
**Low iron with low TIBC** (iron trapped in macrophages)
Long inflammatory illness or cancer; high hepcidin
Target cells, red cell count high for the hemoglobin
Normal or high iron (iron cannot enter heme)
Old paint or firing range; abdominal pain, neuro signs
**Ringed sideroblasts on marrow iron stain**; alcohol, isoniazid, ALAS2

idea.rule: Microcytosis with too much iron (high transferrin saturation and ferritin) = sideroblastic; too little = iron deficiency.
also: Confirm with ringed sideroblasts on marrow iron stain
Causes: X-linked ALAS2 defect, alcohol, isoniazid, lead, copper deficiency

set_title: Swelling of the face and lips: which mechanism
stem: A 34-year-old man has had three episodes of nonpitting, nonitchy swelling of the lips and tongue in the past 4 months, each lasting 2 to 3 days. He has never had hives. He started lisinopril for hypertension 6 months ago. Serum C4 is normal.
oneliner: 34M + recurrent nonitchy lip and tongue swelling + never hives + lisinopril 6 months + C4 normal → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Hereditary angioedema has a **low C4** because C1 is unchecked; his C4 is normal
whyNot.B: Allergic angioedema comes with **itchy wheals**; his swelling is nonitchy and he has never had hives
whyNot.D: Mastocytosis gives **episodic flushing and itching**; he has neither, and the swelling began after a new drug
whyNot.E: Anaphylaxis has **hives, wheeze or hypotension within minutes**; his swellings last days without hives

why: Same man, one change: C4 is normal. With complement intact, the bradykinin excess comes from the drug: **ACE normally breaks down bradykinin**, so the inhibitor lets it build up and cause swelling without wheals that antihistamines will not fix.

head: Hives or itch
C4 level
Trigger
Response to antihistamine or epinephrine
rows: Minor trauma, dental work, stress; family history
None; treat with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant
ACE inhibitor (bradykinin builds up), weeks to years after starting
Allergen such as a sting, food or drug, within minutes

idea.rule: Nonitchy swelling on an ACE inhibitor with normal C4 = drug-induced bradykinin excess; stop the drug.
also: ARBs rarely cause it; neprilysin inhibitors can add to the risk

set_title: Cyanosis or low oxygen content with a normal arterial PO2
stem: A 40-year-old man is found confused with a headache after a night in a closed cabin heated by a propane stove. Pulse oximetry reads 99%. Arterial PO2 is 95 mm Hg and arterial oxygen content is 11 mL/dL. Carbon monoxide poisoning and anemia are both being considered.
oneliner: 40M + confusion and headache after a night near a propane stove + pulse oximetry 99% + PO2 95 + oxygen content 11 mL/dL → carbon monoxide or anemia?
ask: Which single finding favours carbon monoxide poisoning over anemia?

options.A: A rise in dyspnea with exertion
options.B: An arterial PO2 of 95 mm Hg

whyNot.A: **Dyspnea** appears in both when delivery is low
whyNot.B: **A normal PO2** occurs in both, since the lungs are working
whyNot.C: **A normal oximeter reading** occurs in both, because it cannot see carboxyhemoglobin or a low hemoglobin
whyNot.D: **A low content** is present in both

why: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin more than 200 times more tightly than oxygen, lowering content and shifting the curve left, yet the PO2 and oximeter look normal. The **hemoglobin level is normal** (the carboxyhemoglobin level is high), whereas in anemia the hemoglobin itself is low.

head: Arterial PO2
Hemoglobin
Oxygen content and saturation
Blood color and response to oxygen
Heart (echocardiogram)
rows: Content low; pulse oximetry reads about 85% and stays there
**Chocolate-brown blood that stays brown in air; 100% oxygen does not correct it**
Content low; the pulse oximeter reads falsely normal because it cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
**Raised carboxyhemoglobin on co-oximetry**; headache and confusion after a heater or fire; cherry-red skin is uncommon
Blood is red; no cyanosis because little deoxyhemoglobin is present
Low, and does not rise with 100% oxygen (right-to-left shunt)
**Structural defect with a shunt (transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot)**

idea.rule: Normal PO2, low oxygen content: normal hemoglobin with raised carboxyhemoglobin = carbon monoxide; low hemoglobin = anemia.
also: Co-oximetry measures carboxyhemoglobin; the pulse oximeter cannot
Treat with 100% oxygen, hyperbaric if severe
Cherry-red skin is a late and uncommon sign

stem: A 22-year-old woman has vomiting, rapid breathing and agitation. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F) and respirations are 34/min. Serum HCO3- is 11 mEq/L, the anion gap is 22 mEq/L and glucose is 96 mg/dL. Salicylate poisoning and lactic acidosis are both being considered.
oneliner: 22F + vomiting + rapid breathing 34/min + agitation + temp 38.1°C + HCO3- 11, gap 22 + glucose 96 → salicylate poisoning or lactic acidosis?
ask: Which single finding favours salicylate poisoning over lactic acidosis?

options.B: A serum anion gap of 22 mEq/L

whyNot.A: **Fast breathing** is the compensation for acidosis in both
whyNot.D: A **normal glucose** argues against diabetic ketoacidosis but fits both of these
whyNot.E: **Vomiting** occurs in both and does not separate them

why: Salicylate stimulates the medullary respiratory center directly, causing a primary respiratory alkalosis on top of a gap acidosis (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation raises lactate and ketoacids). Cochlear toxicity produces **tinnitus**, which lactic acidosis never causes.

head: Anion gap
Urine anion gap or urine ketones
Setting
Respiratory picture
rows: **Urine anion gap positive** (the kidney cannot excrete ammonium)
Young woman with a stone-forming, hypokalemic distal defect, or diabetic kidney disease with hyperkalemia
**Urine anion gap negative** (the kidney excretes ammonium chloride normally)
Volume depletion, hypokalemia, stool bicarbonate loss
**High, with a very high creatinine and urea nitrogen** (retained phosphate and sulfate)
Advanced chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury
**Ketones in urine and blood, with glucose above 250 mg/dL**
Type 1 diabetes, missed insulin or infection
Ketones may be present; glucose normal
Overdose with tinnitus, vomiting and fever
**Primary respiratory alkalosis together with the gap acidosis**
Shock, sepsis, ischemia, or metformin toxicity

idea.rule: Gap acidosis plus tinnitus and an early respiratory alkalosis = salicylate poisoning.
also: Treat with sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine; hemodialysis if severe
